Understanding goroutines and channels without a deadlock

I am moving from sequential Go to a small worker pipeline. My first version blocked forever because I sent to an unbuffered channel before starting a receiver. This minimal version works, but who should own closing the channel? I want cancellation to remain predictable as the pipeline grows.

The producer should close values after its final send. Receivers normally do not close channels because another producer could still be sending. A range loop stops after the channel is closed and drained.
If you add several producers, wait for all of them with a WaitGroup, then close the channel in a separate goroutine. Cancellation should be a separate signal, usually context.Context.

Fixing a shared-map concurrency bug in my cache

My HTTP cache worked in a small manual test, then crashed under parallel requests with concurrent map writes. I put a mutex around writes. Do I need to protect reads as well? The cache contains immutable strings but the map itself changes whenever an entry expires.
Yes. Reading a map concurrently with a write is unsafe even when the stored values are immutable. Use the same mutex for every access, including deletes and iteration.
Run go test -race against a test that performs reads and writes concurrently. RWMutex can help a read-heavy workload, but measure before choosing it over Mutex.

A small REST API with explicit error responses

I am building a tiny book API using net/http. I want JSON errors, a clear status code, and no accidental write of the default 200 status before validation finishes. Here is the helper I use for invalid input. What should I watch for when adding successful responses?
Set headers before WriteHeader or the first body write. Remember to return from the handler after sending an error; otherwise the success path can append another JSON object.

Wrapping errors while keeping errors.Is useful

I used string comparisons for a missing-record error and they broke as soon as I added context. I have switched to wrapping with %w. I would like the service layer to add helpful context without losing the original sentinel for the handler.
Use %w when the cause should remain inspectable. errors.Is walks the wrapping chain; comparing the complete message cannot do that.
For a typed error containing fields, use errors.As. Think about which errors form part of your package contract so callers do not depend on database-specific errors.

SQLite indexes: why my category feed got slower

My forum feed joins posts, post_categories, and comments. Adding an index on every column made inserts slower and barely improved the feed. I am learning to read the query plan before changing the schema. Which composite index would you inspect first for category filtering?

EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN
SELECT p.id, p.title
FROM post_categories pc
JOIN posts p ON p.id = pc.post_id
WHERE pc.category_id = 2
ORDER BY p.created_at DESC;
Inspect an index beginning with category_id on the join table, such as (category_id, post_id). An existing primary key beginning with post_id does not provide the same access path.
The ORDER BY may still need a temporary sort after the join. Measure representative data and avoid assuming an index on created_at alone will solve the entire query.

Promises and async/await: why my loop finishes early

I expected await items.forEach(async ...) to wait for all requests, but the next line runs immediately. This is a simplified example with a pretend asynchronous formatter. Should I use a for...of loop or Promise.all?
forEach returns undefined and does not collect the promises returned by its callback. Promise.all with map waits for all of them and preserves input order in the results.

A slower response from an old search sometimes replaces results from the newest search. I debounce input but that does not guarantee response order. I am cancelling the previous request when the query changes. Is there anything else the UI should handle?

I used JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(value)) to copy application state. Dates turned into strings and undefined properties vanished. My current state is plain data, but I am trying to understand when structuredClone helps and when it will reject a value.
structuredClone preserves many built-in data types, including Date, Map, Set, and cycles. It cannot clone functions or DOM nodes, so it is not a general object copier.

Making localStorage failure visible without crashing

Private browsing settings and storage limits can make setItem throw. I want my notes tool to remain usable in memory, while clearly telling the visitor that refresh may lose their edits. Is catching writes enough?
Catch reads as well: accessing storage can throw when it is disabled. JSON.parse can also fail, so validate both the syntax and the shape of loaded data.

I was adding clone() whenever the compiler complained. Now I am trying to borrow a string for a read-only operation instead. Is &str the right function parameter when I only need to print the value?
Yes. A &str accepts borrowed string slices without taking ownership of the String. The caller can continue using its allocation after the call.

Vec growth and the difference between length and capacity

I reserved space for 100 elements and was surprised that indexing element zero still panicked. I confused capacity with initialized length. This tiny example helped, but when is with_capacity a worthwhile optimization?
Capacity is allocated space; length counts initialized values. Indexing checks length. reserve and with_capacity do not create elements.
Preallocation is useful when you have a realistic size estimate and repeated growth is measurable. For a fixed initialized length, vec![0; 100] expresses a different operation.

Sharing read-only configuration between threads with Arc

I want several worker threads to share a large immutable configuration. Cloning the full struct into every worker feels wasteful. I am considering Arc rather than a global variable. Is a mutex necessary for read-only access?
For immutable data whose type is Sync, Arc provides shared ownership without a mutex. Arc::clone increments the reference count instead of duplicating the vector.

Why my default hash array was shared between keys
I used Hash.new([]) to group filenames and adding to one category seemed to change another. The default object was the same array. This block version appears to fix it. What makes it different?

files = Hash.new { |hash, key| hash[key] = [] }
files[:ruby] << "app.rb"
files[:go] << "main.go"
p files
The block allocates and stores a fresh array for each missing key. Hash.new([]) reuses one default array and does not automatically store it for the key.
The assignment inside the block matters. A block that merely returns [] gives a fresh array but does not retain it in the hash for subsequent accesses.

I am replacing manual open and close calls with File.open using a block. I understand the syntax, but how does it help if parsing raises before the block finishes? I want resource cleanup to be reliable.

File.open("events.log", "r") do |file|
  file.each_line do |line|
    puts line.strip
  end
end
The block form closes the file when control leaves the block, including when an exception propagates. It centralizes cleanup around the lifetime of the resource.
For a custom resource wrapper, use ensure around yield. Be careful not to rescue every exception and hide a parsing failure just to perform cleanup.

My settings lookup returned nil even though the JSON clearly contained a theme. I used a symbol key, but JSON.parse returns string keys by default. Is symbolizing keys always a good idea?

Benchmarking an O(n²) duplicate check before optimizing syntax

I spent time changing Ruby syntax while the real problem was calling include? on a growing array for every value. A Set makes membership checks easier to express. How should I explain the complexity tradeoff to a beginner?

require "set"
seen = Set.new
duplicate = [3, 1, 3].any? do |value|
  existed = seen.include?(value)
  seen.add(value)
  existed
end
p duplicate
Repeated linear searches can produce quadratic work. A hash-backed Set usually gives average constant-time membership, reducing the overall scan to average linear time.
Mention the extra memory and hashing cost. For tiny arrays the simpler approach may be adequate; for large input the algorithmic difference usually matters more than syntax.

List comprehensions: readable transformations versus clever nesting
I need the squares of non-negative values from a small list. A comprehension is neat here, but nested comprehensions quickly become hard to review. Where do you draw the line?

values = [-3, 0, 2, 5]
squares = [value * value for value in values if value >= 0]
print(squares)
One transformation plus one simple filter is a clear use of a comprehension. If the expression needs a paragraph of explanation, a named helper or ordinary loop is easier to debug.
Use a generator expression if you only need a single aggregate, for example sum(value * value for value in values). That avoids building a separate result list.

The mutable default argument that kept yesterday's data
My helper had items=[] in its signature. Calling it twice without an argument reused the previous list. I know the standard fix is None, but when is the default expression actually evaluated?

def collect(value, items=None):
    if items is None:
        items = []
    items.append(value)
    return items

print(collect(1))
print(collect(2))
Defaults are evaluated when the function definition executes, not on every call. The original list was shared across calls that omitted the parameter.
Use is None rather than if not items. An explicitly provided empty list may be intentional, and truthiness would accidentally replace it.

I am prototyping a command-line task tracker. I want two inserts to succeed together or both be rolled back. Does using the connection as a context manager also close it?

import sqlite3

connection = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
with connection:
    connection.execute("CREATE TABLE tasks (title TEXT NOT NULL)")

My signal calculation produced a dimension error after I changed row vectors into columns. I had used * when I wanted to multiply matching samples. This small example helped me understand the distinction.
.* multiplies corresponding elements, while * performs matrix multiplication. With two 1-by-3 row vectors, a * b is not dimensionally valid.

Tracing a multiplication loop one cell at a time

I am learning Brainfuck by tracing tape state on paper. This program puts 65 in the second cell and outputs A under an ASCII-style byte output convention. I understand the additions but keep losing track of where the pointer ends.
Start with cell zero equal to 8. Each loop iteration moves right, adds 8, returns left, and subtracts 1. After eight iterations the cells are [0, 64] and the pointer is back at cell zero.
The final >+ moves to cell one and increments it to 65 before output. State assumptions about cell width and character encoding when sharing Brainfuck examples.
